conversation.content:
Hi there—my name is Sarah, and I’m a perinatal mental-health clinician. I’m here to check in on how you’re feeling now that your little one has arrived. Over the next few minutes we’ll use a short, well-tested questionnaire called the EPDS (Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale). It’s simply ten questions about the past week, designed to pick up on signs of depression or anxiety that can creep up after childbirth. Everything you share stays between us unless there’s an urgent safety concern, and my only goal is to make sure you feel heard, supported, and safe. When you’re ready, we can start with the first question:

Over the past seven days, how often have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things?

I’ve still been able to laugh sometimes, but it feels like it takes more effort. I’ll smile when my partner makes a joke or when the baby does something cute, yet it doesn’t come as easily or naturally as it used to. Most of the week I guess I’d say “sometimes” rather than “most of the time.”
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

Yeah… sometimes, but not like I used to. I’ll chuckle if my husband pulls a silly face or if the baby makes a funny noise, yet it feels kind of forced—like I have to remind myself to enjoy the moment instead of it just happening naturally.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

I still get little sparks of excitement—like when my mom said she’d come over so I could take a walk by myself—but they’re pretty short-lived. Most of the time I’m just thinking about everything I have to get done, so even the things I used to enjoy feel more like chores on the list than something I truly look forward to.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… a few times this week. When the baby wouldn’t settle at 3 a.m., I kept thinking I must be doing something wrong—maybe I’m not feeding him right or I missed his sleepy cues. My head knows it’s probably normal newborn stuff, but I still catch myself replaying it and feeling like I should have figured it out already.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

I do feel that way—kind of on edge even when everything looks fine on the surface. Like, I’ll be sitting on the couch, baby’s sleeping peacefully, but my mind keeps jumping to “what if he stops breathing?” or “what if I’m missing some sign that he’s sick?” There’s no real reason for it, but the worry just lingers in the background most of the day.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

A couple of times—especially at night—I’ve had this sudden rush of fear, like my heart’s racing and I can’t catch my breath. Nothing’s happening, the house is quiet, but it’s like my body’s sounding an alarm I can’t turn off. It passes after a few minutes, but it leaves me shaky.
Things have been getting on top of me

Most days this week I’ve felt like I’m wading through quick-sand. There’s bottles to wash, laundry piled up, the baby needs changing, and I just think, “How am I supposed to keep up?” I’m managing the basics, but it feels like I’m one step away from everything toppling over.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

Not so much “unhappy” as just… wired. I lie there in the dark after a feed, baby’s snoring away, but my brain keeps spinning through to-do lists and what-ifs. I’ll drift off for maybe an hour, then jolt awake for no clear reason. It’s happening three, four nights a week now, so I’m pretty drained during the day.
I have felt sad or miserable

Yeah, I’ve had stretches—usually in the late afternoon—where I just feel heavy and teary. I wouldn’t call it all-day despair, but a couple of times I’ve caught myself staring out the window feeling like the color’s drained out of everything. It lifts after a bit, but it keeps circling back.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

Only once this week—yesterday, when the baby wouldn’t nap and I couldn’t get the sling adjusted right. I sat on the nursery floor with him crying on my chest and tears just rolled. It wasn’t sobbing, more like quiet leaking, and it stopped once my partner took over for ten minutes.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No—never. I feel overwhelmed sometimes, but I haven’t had any thoughts like that. I just want to feel like myself again so I can take care of my baby.

You've shared that since your baby arrived laughter feels forced, excitement fades fast, and you often catch yourself worrying that something will go wrong even when everything looks calm. You describe late-afternoon sadness, racing thoughts that steal your sleep, and moments of sudden panic that leave you shaky, yet you're still showing up every day for your little one.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 17, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient reports only brief sparks of enjoyment that quickly fade, indicating a noticeable reduction in anticipatory pleasure, aligning with 'Definitely less than I used to'.</sym>, <sym>Patient acknowledges repeated self-blame "a few times this week" with detailed rumination, matching "Yes, some of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes pervasive, intrusive worries that occur "most of the day" without objective triggers, matching "Yes, very often"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes classic panic-like episodes with racing heart and breathlessness occurring multiple times without triggers, matching "Yes, sometimes"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports frequent struggle and feeling overwhelmed, matching "sometimes I haven't been coping as well as usual"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports disrupted sleep 3-4 nights/week due to racing thoughts, matching "Yes, sometimes"</sym>, <sym>Patient experiences frequent, recurring episodes of sadness that feel heavy and color-draining, matching "Yes, quite often."</sym>)
**Reasoning:** A score of 17 places you well above the ≥14 threshold indicating probable major <med>depressive disorder with peripartum onset</med>. Key endorsements include diminished enjoyment most days, pervasive worries, panic-type surges, self-reproach about mothering, and recurrent tearfulness, together meeting <med>DSM-5</med> criteria for frequency and functional impact. No self-harm ideation was endorsed. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent appointment with your <med>obstetrician</med>, <med>midwife</med>, or <med>primary care provider</med> to review results and discuss treatment options
2. Ask about evidence-based therapies such as <med>interpersonal therapy</med> or <med>CBT</med> tailored for postpartum mood
3. Discuss possible benefits and risks of <med>antidepressant medication</med> compatible with breastfeeding if applicable
4. Plan daily 20-30 minute walks or light movement to help regulate mood and sleep
5. Share screening results with a trusted support person so they can help monitor your wellbeing
6. Use brief breathing or grounding exercises when you notice the racing heart or spiraling thoughts
7. Schedule a follow-up EPDS in 1-2 weeks to track any changes
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 17: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Note  
Date of contact: [today’s date]  
Source: Patient self-report on 10-item Edinburgh-based questionnaire  

1. Primary symptoms endorsed  
   – Marked reduction in capacity for spontaneous enjoyment and humor; pleasure when noted feels effortful  
   – Loss of anticipatory excitement; previously enjoyable activities now experienced as tasks  
   – Frequent unprovoked worries (“baby will stop breathing”), occasional nocturnal panic episodes (HR racing, breathlessness)  
   – Persistent self-blame regarding infant care despite objective adequacy  
   – Recurrent late-afternoon tearfulness and emotional heaviness  
   – Sleep-onset and maintenance problems unrelated to infant needs; racing thoughts  
   – Global sense of being “on edge” and overwhelmed most days  

2. Pattern consistency  
   Answers cluster around:  
   • Anhedonia / low positive affect (Items 1, 2)  
   • Cognitive-emotional anxiety (Items 4, 5)  
   • Self-critical rumination with guilt (Item 3)  
   • Mood-congruent insomnia and crying (Items 7, 9)  
   • Functional strain but maintenance of basic infant care (Item 6)  

3. Screening significance  
   Meets provisional cut-score concern for postpartum depression and co-occurring anxiety; differential includes perinatal generalized anxiety disorder and adjustment disorder with mixed mood features.  

4. Risk factors identified  
   – Perinatal anhedonia, guilt, frequent crying  
   – Mood-related insomnia ≥3 nights/week  
   – Panic-type episodes without medical trigger  
   – No suicidal ideation, intent, or self-harm thoughts reported; protective factor: strong infant-focused motivation  

5. Safety  
   Denies any thoughts of self-harm. No current suicidal ideation; no plan or intent.  

Summary: Screening indicates clinically significant depressive and anxious symptoms of perinatal onset. Denies self-harm. Recommend completion of formal EPDS and expedited perinatal mental-health evaluation for confirmation, psycho-education, and discussion of evidence-based options.
